lessons.title: Marketing Is the Act of Making Change
lessons.key_idea: Marketing is not shouting or manipulating but the generous work of helping people become who they want to become.

lessons.title: Find Your Smallest Viable Market
lessons.key_idea: Instead of trying to reach everyone, choose the smallest group you can truly delight and serve them so well they can't imagine life without you.

lessons.title: People Don't Want What You Want
lessons.key_idea: Empathy means understanding that others have different worldviews, and you must tell stories that fit what they already believe.

lessons.title: Claim an Edge Nobody Else Owns
lessons.key_idea: Map your market on two axes that your audience cares about and position yourself at an extreme where competitors aren't.

lessons.title: Status and Tension Drive Every Decision
lessons.key_idea: People act when you create a healthy tension between where they are and where they could be, often tied to their sense of status.

lessons.title: People Like Us Do Things Like This
lessons.key_idea: Culture and belonging are powerful forces, so lasting change happens when you help a group adopt a new shared norm.

lessons.title: Earn Trust, Then Keep Showing Up
lessons.key_idea: By asking who it's for and what it's for, then earning permission and keeping your promises consistently, you build trust that turns customers into your marketers.

plan.title: This Is Marketing
plan.author: Seth Godin
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's core arguments and structure well, though I may not recall every specific anecdote, so lessons rely on its central, well-established ideas.
plan.one_liner: Forget hype and shouting: real marketing is the generous act of helping people change for the better.
plan.summary: Seth Godin argues that marketing is not about advertising, hype, or tricking people into buying. It is the generous work of helping people solve a problem and become who they hope to become. Instead of chasing everyone, he urges you to choose a smallest viable market: a specific group whose worldview you understand and whose needs you can serve better than anyone else. From there, you position your work on the edges others ignore, tell stories that match what your audience already believes, and create the tension that makes change feel worth it. Godin shows how status, belonging, and the idea that people like us do things like this drive almost every decision. The goal is to earn permission and trust over time, so the people you serve come to depend on you and spread the word for you.
